183.title: Upright, not propped up
183.hook: honor the divine spark within you and stand upright, not held upright (Meditations 3.5, 3.12)
183.howItsDone: In the Stoic tradition, the daimon is the guiding reason within each person, and readers of Marcus often use 3.5 and 3.12 as a daily check on honesty and self-reliance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cracked loaf: Marcus found beauty in bread split at the surface. Your line was the cracked loaf. What imperfect thing looked alive to you? Day one hundred eighty-three.

A tomato plant tied to a stake grows tall, but only because something holds it up. Cut the string, and it flops. A young oak in a field has nothing holding it. It sways in the wind and stays standing. Plenty of people are a bit of both. We lean on praise to feel good, on other people's calm to feel calm, on someone's approval to feel sure we did the right thing. Marcus noticed that in himself, and he wrote a short, blunt sentence about it. Today's word is his name for what holds you up from the inside: daimon.
screen: `A TOMATO PLANT ON A STAKE.` → `AN OAK IN A FIELD.` → `DAIMON.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Daimon is Greek, and it does not mean demon. That dark meaning came much later. For Marcus, the daimon is the divine spirit within each person, a fragment, he says elsewhere, of the reason that orders the whole universe, given to each of us as a guide. Your inner compass. Your best mind. The Greek word for happiness, eudaimonia, literally means having a good daimon, and Marcus plays on that himself. So in 3.5 he tells himself: let the god within you be the guardian of who you are. Be cheerful. Don't look for help from outside, or for the calm that other people give you. And then, in George Long's translation: "A man then must stand erect, not be kept erect by others." Upright, not propped up. In 3.12 he adds how. Do the work in front of you seriously, calmly, following reason, keeping your divine part pure, as if you might have to give it back at any moment. Expect nothing and fear nothing. And be honest in every word. That's the key: honesty. A propped-up person has to manage what everyone thinks. An upright person just has to be true. You don't need to believe in a daimon the way Marcus did to use this. Religious listeners may hear the soul, or conscience, or God's breath in a person. Others hear integrity. The question is the same: when the string is cut, what holds you up? Marcus's answer is the thing inside that doesn't lie. Stand on that. Upright, not propped.
screen: `DAIMON: NOT A DEMON.` · `THE DIVINE GUIDE WITHIN.` · `STAND ERECT, NOT KEPT ERECT.` · `HONEST IN EVERY WORD.` · then, large: `UPRIGHT, NOT PROPPED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare to do one thing with full honesty. Settle, and sit up tall, spine upright, nothing leaning. Breathe. Think of something coming up today where you might shade the truth a little to be liked: a compliment you don't mean, a yes you mean as no, a story you'd polish. Decide now to say it straight, kindly and plainly. Notice what it's like to be held up from the inside. The bell holds the time.
Daimon. Greek for the divine spirit within a person, for Marcus the inner guide to honor; not a demon. Today's word.
Your line: upright, not propped. Today, do the honest thing you chose, and notice whether you need anyone's approval afterward to feel all right. Day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: The merchant and the parrot
184.hook: a caged parrot asks its merchant to greet the wild parrots of India (Masnavi 1.1547ff)
184.howItsDone: The merchant and the parrot is a story from the Masnavi's first book; Sufi teachers read the caged parrot as the soul and the parrots of India as the free friends of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daimon: Marcus told himself to stand upright, not propped up. Did you say the honest thing? Day one hundred eighty-four, the last day of the week.

Somebody you love is going somewhere you can't. A cousin flying back to the country your family came from. A friend going home to the town you both grew up in. And you say, without thinking: say hi to everyone for me. Tell them I miss them. It's a small line, but it carries a lot. It says: part of me belongs there. Rumi's next story starts with that exact request. A rich merchant is getting ready for a long trip to India, and before he goes, he makes the rounds of his household. Today, the merchant and the parrot.
screen: `SAY HI TO EVERYONE FOR ME.` → `A MERCHANT BOUND FOR INDIA.` → `THE MERCHANT AND THE PARROT.`

segments.voice: The merchant is generous. He asks every servant and every member of the household: what shall I bring you from India? Each one names something. And then he comes to his parrot. It's a beautiful bird, and a clever one, and it lives in a cage in his house. What gift do you want? The parrot asks for no gift at all. It asks for a message to be carried. When you see the parrots of India, it says, flying free in the forests, give them my greeting. Tell them a parrot who longs for them is shut in a cage in my house, by the turning of fate. Ask them: is it right that I waste away here while you fly among the trees? Is this what friends do? Remember me, it says, when you're in the meadows at dawn. That's the whole request. Greet them for me. Rumi stops the story here for long reflections, and Sufi readers take the caged parrot as the human soul, kept in the cage of the body and this world, and the wild parrots as the saints, the friends of God, who are already free. That message is the soul's longing, sent home. You can hear the reed from earlier in this camp again: cut from the reedbed, and crying for it. Now look back at the week. In Rumi's story, the lion argued for tying the camel, a hare walked slowly on purpose, and the lion drowned fighting his own face, while Rumi pointed to the lion inside. In Marcus's notebook, cracked bread had its own beauty, and a person could stand upright, not propped. Two books, kept apart, and the week ends with a small caged bird asking only to be remembered. Tomorrow, his message arrives in India, and something happens nobody expected.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send a message to someone far. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who's far away: across the country, across an ocean, or just across a silence that's grown too long. What would you want them to hear? Not news. Just: I remember you. I miss you. I'm still here. Hold those words for a minute. Then, if you can, actually send it after the bell. The bell holds the time.
The merchant and the parrot. A caged parrot asks for no gift, only that its master greet the free parrots of India for it. Today's word.
screen: `THE MERCHANT AND THE PARROT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: greet them for me. Today, send the words you held, even one line, to someone far away. Day one hundred eighty-four.

185.title: The parrot drops
185.hook: hearing the caged parrot's words, a wild parrot falls as if dead, and the merchant reports it home (Masnavi 1)
185.howItsDone: Teachers of the Masnavi often pause at this scene to discuss Rumi's reflections on speech, that words spoken cannot be taken back, before continuing the parrot's story.

segments.voice: Last week ended with a caged parrot asking the merchant: greet them for me. Did your message reach someone far away? Day one hundred eighty-five, and a new week.

You send a text you think is harmless. A joke, a bit of news, a passing comment. And then the little dots appear, and disappear, and appear again. And you realize, too late, that your words landed like a stone. Words can do things we never meant them to do. The merchant arrives in India. He finds the forests, and the parrots, flashing green in the trees. And, faithful to his promise, he delivers his parrot's message. Today, the parrot drops.
screen: `A HARMLESS TEXT LANDS LIKE A STONE.` → `THE FORESTS OF INDIA.` → `THE PARROT DROPS.`

segments.voice: The merchant stands under the trees and repeats his parrot's words exactly: a parrot who loves you is shut in a cage in my house; is it right that it wastes away while you fly free? And as soon as he's finished, one of the wild parrots begins to tremble. It shakes, loses its grip, and falls from the branch to the ground. Still. As if dead. The merchant is horrified. What have I done? he says. I've killed a creature with a sentence. Maybe this bird and mine were kin, as close as body and soul. Why did I ever carry that message? Rumi stops here to reflect. Words, he says, are like flint and steel: what springs from the tongue is fire. Once spoken, they're like an arrow already shot; you can't call them back. They travel, and they do things in the world, often things you didn't intend. So guard your tongue. But notice the other side too. Those words did something no gift could have done. They moved a wild bird so deeply it fell from the tree. Words are powerful precisely because they reach inside. The merchant finishes his trading, sad, and goes home. He hands out the gifts. And then the parrot in its cage says: and my gift? What did you see? What did you say? The merchant doesn't want to answer. He's ashamed. He knows the story will hurt. But he tells it. And we'll see tomorrow what those words do next. For today, just this: every message does something. Words travel, and they act.
screen: `HIS PARROT'S WORDS, EXACTLY.` · `A WILD PARROT FALLS, AS IF DEAD.` · `WORDS ARE FIRE, AN ARROW SHOT.` · `AND MY GIFT? WHAT DID YOU SAY?` · then, large: `EVERY MESSAGE DOES SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how news changes things. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a message that changed your day: good news, bad news, a single sentence from someone. Where were you? What happened in your body when you heard it? Then think of a message you sent that did more than you expected, for good or for ill. Just notice the power in both directions. Words travel. The bell holds the time.
The parrot drops. In India a wild parrot hears the caged one's message and falls as if dead, and the ashamed merchant must report it home. Today's word.
Your line: what the message did. Today, before you send one message, read it once as the person receiving it, and ask what it will do. Day one hundred eighty-five.

186.title: Played dead, flew free
186.hook: the caged parrot copies it, is thrown out of the cage, and flies (Masnavi 1)
186.howItsDone: Sufi teachers often read the merchant and the parrot as a lesson in fana, the passing away of the ego, and quote the saying 'die before you die' in explaining it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the parrot drops: a wild parrot in India heard the caged one's words and fell from the tree. Did you read a message as its receiver before sending? Day one hundred eighty-six.

Plenty of people have a version of themselves they perform. The funny one at parties. The one who's always fine. The high achiever, the helper, the cool one who doesn't care. It started as a gift, maybe. People loved it. And slowly it became a cage, because now we have to keep performing, or they won't love us anymore. The merchant is home. His parrot has asked what happened in India. Ashamed, he tells it: a wild parrot heard your greeting, trembled, and fell down dead. Today, played dead.
screen: `THE SELF WE PERFORM.` → `A GIFT THAT BECAME A CAGE.` → `PLAYED DEAD.`

segments.voice: As soon as the merchant finishes, his own parrot begins to tremble. It shakes in the cage, falls from its perch, and lies there, stiff and still. The merchant is shattered. He cries out, tears his clothes, and mourns for his sweet-voiced bird, the companion of his days. Rumi gives him a long, aching lament. Then, heartbroken, he opens the cage door and lifts the little body out and lets it drop. And the parrot flies. Straight up to a high branch, alive and free. The stunned merchant calls up: what just happened? And the parrot explains. That wild parrot in India wasn't dead. It was sending me advice, by what it did. It was saying: your beautiful voice, your charm, the way you delight everyone, that's what put you in the cage. Let it go. Become as if dead, and you'll be set free. The parrot says goodbye to its master kindly, and flies away. Rumi's lesson: the thing that makes people admire us can be the very thing that traps us. Sufis have a saying for this, which they attribute to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: die before you die. Hadith scholars say it isn't found in the recognized collections, though Sufi teachers treasure it. It doesn't mean harming yourself in any way. It means letting the grasping, performing self fall still, the ego we met with the lion inside, so that something truer can live. The parrot didn't stop being a parrot. It stopped performing, and it flew. Die before you die.
screen: `THE CAGED PARROT FALLS STILL.` · `THROWN OUT, IT FLIES FREE.` · `YOUR CHARM PUT YOU IN THE CAGE.` · `LET THE PERFORMING SELF FALL STILL.` · then, large: `DIE BEFORE YOU DIE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one act you perform for others. Settle, and breathe. Ask: what do I do mostly so people will like me, or see me a certain way? Always being upbeat. Always having an answer. Pretending not to care. Pick one. Now imagine, just for today, letting it go still. Not dramatically. Just not doing it. Notice what's underneath it. It may be tender. That's all right. The bell holds the time.
Played dead. The caged parrot copies the wild one, falls still, is thrown out of its cage, and flies free: letting the performing self go. Today's word.
Your line: die before you die. Today, in one conversation, drop the act you chose, and let yourself be a little more plainly you. Day one hundred eighty-six.

187.title: The inner retreat
187.hook: Marcus: people seek retreats by the sea, but you can retire into your own mind at any hour (Meditations 4.3)
187.howItsDone: Many readers of the Meditations practice 4.3 as a short pause during the day, withdrawing into a few steadying thoughts, and modern Stoic practice often calls it the inner citadel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the caged parrot played dead and flew free. Your line was die before you die. Which act did you let fall still? Day one hundred eighty-seven.

Everybody has a dream escape. A cabin in the mountains. A week on a beach with no phone. A little house by a lake where nobody can reach you. We scroll through pictures of them at our desks. We count the days until vacation. And then the vacation comes, and on the second day, lying by the water, we're still replaying the argument from work. An emperor who could have had any villa in the Roman world noticed this too. And he wrote down where he thought the real retreat was. Today, the inner retreat.
screen: `A CABIN, A BEACH, A LAKE.` → `STILL REPLAYING THE ARGUMENT.` → `THE INNER RETREAT.`

segments.voice: Meditations 4.3 begins, in George Long's translation: "Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains." And Marcus admits he wants them too, very much. But then he pushes back on himself. You can, he says, whenever you choose, retire into yourself. Nowhere is quieter, or freer from trouble, than your own mind, especially if you have in it certain thoughts that bring calm the moment you look at them. Then he gives the instruction plainly: "Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself." Keep the principles short, he says, so they're ready. And he names two of them. First, things out in the world don't reach inside you by themselves; your trouble comes from the opinion you form about them. Second, everything you see is changing and will soon be gone. We'll open that second one tomorrow. Notice what kind of retreat this is. It's not an escape from your life. It's a room inside your life, one you can step into on a crowded train or in a hospital waiting room or in the middle of a hard meeting, and come out renewed. Yesterday Rumi's parrot found freedom by letting the performing self fall still. Today Marcus finds it by stepping inward for a moment. Different traditions, different words, and neither needs the other. But both say the cage and the country house aren't the final word. There's somewhere to go that no one can take from you. The inner retreat.
screen: `HOUSES, SEA-SHORES, MOUNTAINS.` · `RETIRE INTO YOURSELF, ANY HOUR.` · `KEEP THE PRINCIPLES SHORT.` · `A ROOM INSIDE YOUR LIFE.` · then, large: `THE INNER RETREAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a one-minute retreat. Settle, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Imagine stepping through a door into a quiet room inside you. Nobody else can come in. Take one short thought in with you, something steadying: this will pass, or I am here, or only this moment. Breathe slowly. Rest there. When the bell comes, step back out, renewed, into wherever you are. The bell holds the time.
The inner retreat. Marcus in Meditations 4.3: instead of seeking the seaside, retire into your own mind at any hour, and come back renewed. Today's word.
Your line: the inner retreat. Today, in the busiest moment you have, take one minute, step inward, and come back. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

188.title: Nature loves change
188.hook: nothing is more natural than change, Marcus writes (Meditations 4.36)
188.howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often keep a short line like this one in view, and some make a habit of pausing to notice change in small things, such as the breath or the light, as Marcus advised himself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said you don't need the seaside to get away: you can step back into your own mind at any hour. Your line was the inner retreat. Did you take one, even for a minute? Day one hundred eighty-eight.

Find an old photo of yourself. Ten years old, maybe, squinting at the camera. The haircut is gone, the house may be gone, the people holding the camera may be gone. And still, when a gray hair shows up, or a favorite café closes, or a friend moves across the country, something in us says: this isn't supposed to happen. It's easy to treat change like a malfunction. Marcus Aurelius wrote a note to himself about exactly that. Today: nature loves change.
screen: `AN OLD PHOTO OF YOU.` → `CHANGE FEELS LIKE A MALFUNCTION.` → `NATURE LOVES CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Marcus was a Roman emperor, and he wrote his private notes in Greek. The book's own headings place parts of it in army camps. We call them the Meditations. In Book Four he tells himself to keep watching how everything comes about through change, and then he adds a surprising line. In George Long's old translation, the nature of the universe "loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them." Notice the word loves. Marcus doesn't say nature puts up with change, or suffers it. Change is what nature most enjoys doing. The things that exist now, he goes on, are seeds of what will come from them. Marcus quotes Heraclitus elsewhere, the older Greek thinker remembered for saying that everything flows. And later, in Book Seven, Marcus makes it ordinary. Are you afraid of change? Nothing can happen without it. You can't take a warm bath unless the wood changes in the fire. You can't eat unless the food changes in you. The very things that keep you alive are changes. So Marcus isn't asking himself to like every loss. He's asking something smaller and harder: to stop treating change as an insult, as if the universe had broken its promise. It never promised to stay still. Your line for today: change is natural.
screen: `PRIVATE NOTES, IN GREEK.` · `IT LOVES NOTHING SO MUCH AS TO CHANGE.` · `THE BATH NEEDS THE WOOD TO BURN.` · then, large: `CHANGE IS NATURAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing changing. Settle where you are. Pick something small and close: your breath going in and out, the light on the wall, a sound that rises and fades, the warmth of your hands. Just watch it change. You don't have to fix it or hold it. If a bigger change in your life comes to mind, let it sit beside the small one for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Nature loves change. Marcus wrote that the universe loves nothing so much as changing what is and making new things like it. Today's word.
Your line: change is natural. Today, when something shifts that you didn't ask for, say the line once before you react. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

189.title: The old harper
189.hook: an old musician, abandoned by his audience, plays for God alone in a graveyard (Masnavi 1.1913ff)
189.howItsDone: Readers of the Masnavi often read its stories slowly, a section at a time, and in Sufi circles this story is told as a picture of doing good work for God alone, not for praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus wrote that nature loves change. Your line was change is natural. What changed around you yesterday, and how did you meet it? Day one hundred eighty-nine.

The wedding singer everybody once wanted. The athlete twenty years after the last game. Anyone who was once very good at something, and then the calls stopped. Applause is a kind of food, and when it goes, the hunger can be hard to admit. Yesterday Marcus told us change is natural. Today Rumi tells a story about what someone does after that kind of change, when the crowd has gone home for good. It's the first of three days with one character. Today: the old harper.
screen: `WHEN THE CALLS STOP.` → `APPLAUSE IS A KIND OF FOOD.` → `THE OLD HARPER.`

segments.voice: The story is in Book One of the Masnavi, Rumi's long poem of stories. In the days of Umar, the second caliph after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, there lived a harper in Medina. Rumi says his voice was so lovely it made nightingales lose their senses, and one breath of his song could make a gathering feel alive. Then he grew old. His voice cracked. His hands got stiff. Rumi describes the voice that once charmed hearts as now so harsh that nobody wanted it. The invitations stopped. He had no money, and he had nothing else he knew how to do. So one day he took his harp and walked out of the city to the graveyard. And there, among the graves, where no one could hear, he played. Rumi has him say something like this: all my life you gave me breath, and I spent it on others. Now I'll play for you, God, and you'll have to be my patron, because no one else will pay. He played and wept until he fell asleep with his head on a grave, the harp as his pillow. Notice what's happened. He's playing badly, alone, for an audience he can't see. For the first time in his life, the playing isn't for applause. The song has nowhere to go but upward. Some readers hear themselves in him: everything we do for someone to notice, and the strange freedom of doing one thing for no one at all. What happens next is tomorrow. For now, stay with him in the graveyard, playing. Your line: play for no one.
